title: How a WhatsApp Group of 500 Engineers Is Guiding Nepal's Desperate Tunnel Rescue
excerpt: A messaging group set up before the August 26 disaster has become an unlikely lifeline, sharing tunnel blueprints and worker locations as rescue teams search for hundreds still missing.
body:
• A WhatsApp group of more than 500 engineers is providing real-time tunnel layouts and access drawings to rescue workers searching for survivors at six devastated hydropower plants in Nepal's Trishuli valley.
  • Two workers were pulled alive from the Upper Trishuli 3A tunnel on Friday, nine days after the August 26 glacier collapse, in the first confirmed rescue from the underground infrastructure.
  • About 900 workers remain missing from 12 hydropower projects, with an estimated 500 believed trapped in tunnels buried under 2.2 million tonnes of mud and debris.
  • The disaster wiped out 10% of Nepal's electricity generation capacity, with at least 1,287 people killed and more than 5,080 still unaccounted for.

When rescue workers needed to find their way into the buried tunnels of Nepal's Chilime hydropower plant on Saturday, a government official typed a simple request into a WhatsApp chat: "Can you send me Chilime layout drawings."

Within minutes, an engineer in the group responded with detailed drawings of the project's powerhouse and access tunnels, according to Reuters, which reviewed the exchange and spoke with a dozen people involved in the rescue.

A Pre-Existing Network Repurposed for Disaster

The messaging group was originally set up by engineers working across Nepal's expanding hydropower sector before the August 26 glacier collapse sent a wall of water, mud, and rock crashing through the Trishuli valley. Since the disaster, it has been expanded to more than 500 members — engineers, government officials, military personnel, and former plant employees — and has become a critical tool alongside helicopters and heavy machinery.

Members have shared tunnel blueprints, powerhouse layouts, and technical schematics of the buried facilities. Former employees have been consulted through the group about tunnel networks they once worked in. Members have also posted names and mobile phone numbers of missing workers, asking government officials to relay them to telecom authorities to trace their last recorded locations.

First Survivors Emerge After Nine Days

The rescue effort scored its first success on Friday when two workers — mechanical foreman Sanjay Sah and supervisor Kabir Maharjan — were pulled alive from a tunnel at the Upper Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, nine days after the disaster. Both were taken to a military hospital in Kathmandu, where Maharjan cannot move his hands or legs but Sah's injuries are not considered critical.

"The flood has altered the terrain around the tunnels and changed their structure, while mud, rocks, soil and other debris had accumulated inside. This is not a normal closure of tunnels."

— Raja Ram Basnet, Nepal army spokesperson

Rescue teams took almost six days simply to reach the Upper Trishuli 3A tunnel because its entrance was buried beneath debris. Before the breakthrough, they had been pumping oxygen through pipes into cavities in case workers were trapped inside.

Hundreds Still Missing Underground

The scale of the search is staggering. About 900 workers remain unaccounted for across six hydropower plants in the valley, at least three of which were under construction when the flood hit. At the Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant further south, rescue workers penetrated 250 metres into one tunnel before hitting a complete blockage. Officials believe 46 people may be trapped in a chamber where they could have access to food and water.

At the Chilime plant near the Chinese border, at least eight people are believed trapped. Reuters images showed a tunnel entrance with flood debris piled nearly to the ceiling just inside.

Survivors Recount Harrowing Escapes

Jan Jiwan Thakur, a civil engineer at the Upper Trishuli 1 plant, said a colleague warned him moments before the flood swept down the valley, giving him enough time to climb to higher ground with about 100 others.

"We just ran away towards the hillside and, after two to three minutes, when we looked down, everything was gone. The flood debris had entirely covered our office area."

— Jan Jiwan Thakur, civil engineer

Dhan Bahadur Tamang described escaping through a tunnel at the same plant, navigating past rushing pipes and equipment. He and several others used their knowledge of the tunnel system to find a way out, though he described seeing dead bodies during his subterranean escape.

A Devastating Toll on Nepal's Energy Future

The disaster, caused by a glacier collapse, has killed at least 1,287 people, with more than 5,080 still missing. China has reported 21 dead and 541 missing in Tibet. The flood destroyed or damaged 12 hydropower projects across Nepal's Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, wiping out 10% of the country's electricity generation capacity.

Rescue efforts are being led by the Nepali army and police, with assistance from experts from India, South Korea, and China. As search operations continue, family members wait for news. Rajesh Shrestha, whose 30-year-old son Rajish is an environmental engineer at Upper Trishuli 1, holds onto hope.

"Whenever I look outside, I imagine seeing him carrying a bag and coming home, just as he used to," Shrestha said. "I am surviving on the hope that he will return."
image_caption: A WhatsApp group of over 500 engineers is providing tunnel layouts and access drawings to rescue workers at six devastated hydropower sites in Nepal.
nri_angle: India is among the countries assisting Nepal's rescue operations, and the disaster highlights infrastructure vulnerabilities across South Asia's growing hydropower sector.
